bio.en: Alisa Cohn is an executive coach who has worked with C-suite leaders at startups like Etsy, Venmo, and DraftKings as well as Fortune 500s like Microsoft and Google, and has been named one of the world's top startup coaches.
bio.zh: Alisa Cohn 是一位高管教练，曾辅导 Etsy、Venmo、DraftKings 等初创公司以及微软、谷歌等世界 500 强企业的高管，被誉为全球顶尖的初创公司教练之一。

summary.en: Alisa shares specific language for having difficult conversations, such as delivering a tough “no promotion” message while preserving hope and the employee's growth. She pushes back on the idea that a leader's job is to make everyone happy, arguing that driving toward results sometimes requires uncomfortable feedback. The conversation also covers practical tactics for running more effective meetings and a simple three-question routine to close them well.

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Okay, about making things worse or about their reaction?

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 让人 upset。好。你不孤单。再问一个。如果他们 sad 和 upset 有什么问题？那对你意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I love this life coaching we're doing. Yeah, so it's like what happens if they get sad and upset?

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah.

turns.zh: 我觉得是我得处理的东西。突然这个 drama、我得想的新 fire。是它创造的额外工作，而且就，不知道。好问题。

(00:07:51): No one wants to make anybody upset, but through that upset on the other side of that, can often be a whole new possibility and a whole new revelation, and actually a lot of joy and freedom. turns.zh: 你可以再想想对吧？我现在不 put 你 on the spot，但对所有人说，它们难的原因——如你所说——难。但我们一直在给事物加 meaning，每天一直，我觉得很重要、实际上对激励你进行难对话有帮助、也对帮它们走好有帮助。如果你能到底你在上面加了什么、你 weighted 了什么，因为我能理解——你不孤单。我不想让人 upset。完全。(00:07:20)：而且另一方面，当你 enlighten 别人或和人解决一个情况、它难，如果你不给他们机会听你说的、你不提，那你永远没机会帮他们看不同或帮他们改进或帮你改进关系或你想做什么。所以我能理解那是自然的。我不想让他们 upset。(00:07:51)：没人想让任何人 upset，但通过那个 upset，另一面可以是全新可能性和全新 revelation，其实很多 joy 和 freedom。我觉得我们忘了难对话出来的所有其他可能性，就 land 在这些真的不舒服的部分如「哦会很多额外工作」或「他们会不舒服甚至可能哭」。我觉得 tap 进你 make 它 mean 什么、然后还有什么其他可能性很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And it's one thing to hear that and say that, it's another to actually feel that deeply and feel like I shouldn't be as worried as I am. turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes. And as you say that, one of the other fears I have is them just disagreeing and me feeling like maybe it's not right, maybe I'm wrong and feeling shit maybe. I didn't see something and then just looking worse after the whole thing.
turns.zh: 对。如你所说，我另一个怕是他们就不同意、我觉得也许我不对、我错了、感觉糟。我没看到什么、然后之后整体看起来更糟。

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah. turns.zh: 对。所以很有帮助的、我们可以聊的过程的一部分是：难对话第一是 tap 进什么让你不舒服。第二是把心态摆正。说明显的，你做这个是为了伤人感情吗？不，从不，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The opposite.
turns.zh: 相反。

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: That's not the reason that anyone's doing it. But at the end of the day, the hope is as a manager, the reason that you're giving someone this so-called constructive feedback is because you're helping them get better. You need them to change the behavior. They'll never get promoted if they keep doing that. They'll never be successful if they keep doing that. And so, it's your job as a leader and as a manager, to help them out of that problem and help them do something different.
turns.zh: 那不是任何人做的原因。有时人给绩效反馈或谈困扰他们的事是为了表达自己、vent。其实识别那个很有帮助——那是你为什么做。然后也许那时不 做，直到你能 transform 你的理由。但最终希望是作为 manager 你给这个所谓建设性反馈是因为你帮他们变好。你需要他们改行为。他们一直那样永远升不了。他们一直那样永远成功不了。所以你作为 leader 和 manager 的工作是帮他们出那个问题、帮他们做不同的事。

So I wanted to let you know about this. I want to certainly hear what you have to say, but the most important thing is that we leave this discussion knowing how you're going to make sure that you're keeping your peers in the loop and also your team in the loop."
turns.zh: 好，我们从绩效反馈开始，就取个典型例子。首先你做了心态工作、知道你在做什么后，你真想能 mouth 包住那些词。那看起来是练习，话术可以是「你知道 Matilda，我想和你聊聊你跟同级互动的方式。我从他们那里听到的是你经常错过截止日期、不让他们知道你错过了，而且你没完全让团队跟上速度。(00:13:27)：所以他们有点困惑跑来跑去。我们俩都知道你在这里成功、达成目标的最重要方式是确保你以一种一致的方式和同级 work、他们能指望你、你能指望他们。所以我想让你知道这个。我当然想听你说什么，但最重要的是我们离开这个讨论时知道你怎么确保让同级和团队 in the loop。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's so many elements there that are really interesting. Just focusing on what I'm hearing versus just coming from you or something you've done wrong. It's, here's what I'm hearing from multiple sources. I think that helps people. Okay, it's not just you and just like, "Oh, my manager hates me."
turns.zh: 对，那里有那么多有趣元素。就聚焦「我听到的」vs 只来自你或你做错什么。是「我从多个来源听到的」。我觉得那帮人。好，不只是你、不只「我 manager 恨我」。

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like, "Okay, other people are saying this." And then I love this phrase of, we both know where it's not just me telling you this. It's like, "You also know this. I know you're smart and you also know that this is, something is wrong here." And then this goal of, here's what we need to [inaudible 00:14:31]. You're like very clear call to action, almost action item, like leave this meeting with, "Let's just be aligned on this thing."
turns.zh: 就像「好，别人也这么说。」然后我爱这个短语「我们俩都知道」，不是只我告诉你。是「你也知道这个。我知道你聪明、你也知道这里有什么不对。」然后这个目标「这是我们需要……」你非常清晰 call to action，几乎 action item，带着「让我们在离开时对齐这个。」

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah, thanks for calling those out. I hope, and again, what I'm trying to convey in my tone is also, "You know what? It's Tuesday. We got to have this conversation. I'm sure it's going to end well. I'm not mad." The whole point about my manager hates me, right? "I'm not yelling at you." The more even keeled and even matter of fact you can be about something that's kind of just run-of-the-mill feedback, the better. And I think it's just also what I didn't say before, and I think it's also important is that, as you are recognizing that one of your jobs is to give this feedback, is that you have to build a relationship with people so they can hear you through the lens of, "Oh, Alisa wants to help me." Not, "Oh, Alisa hates me. It's always a problem."
turns.zh: 对，谢谢你指出那些。我希望，再说一次我 tone 里试图传达的是「你知道吗，是周二。我们得谈。我相信会结束好。我没生气。」关于我 manager 恨我那个，对吧？「我没在吼你。」你能对这种就是普通反馈越 even-keeled、越 matter-of-fact 越好。我觉得我没之前说的、也重要的是，你认识到你的工作之一是给这个反馈时，你得和人建关系让他们能透过「哦 Alisa 想帮我」的镜头听你。不是「哦 Alisa 恨我。总是问题。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did you start that phrase again? Because the starting is always the hardest part for me. How do you kick off the conversation? What was the couple sentences used?
turns.zh: 你开始那句怎么说的？因为开始对我来说最难。你怎么开启对话？那几句是什么？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: I wanted to have a conversation with you about some things I've been hearing from your peers about the way that you all are interacting together.
turns.zh: 我想和你聊聊我从你同级那里听到的一些关于你们互动方式的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So there's an element of, don't make it feel like a huge deal. Just like, "I want to have this conversation with you about something." And it's just like, "Let's have this conversation and here's what we want to leave this conversation with."
turns.zh: 太好了。所以有个元素，别让它感觉是 huge deal。就「我想和你谈一个事」。然后是「让我们谈，这是我们想带着离开的。」

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yes. And I can't stress enough that it's actually really helpful to also have spent some time with Matilda or whoever saying, "Great job on the way that project landed." Or, "Hey, launches, when they happen on time and they're smooth, sometimes we don't notice anything. I want you to notice, we didn't notice anything. That's fantastic. You did a good job in that launch," or whatever it is. Because then, you've had the conversation with them to give them positive feedback and point out what's working, that builds the relationship so that you have the lens of, "Oh, yeah. When something's working, they tell me. When something's not working, they tell me, too." That's how you build trust as well.
turns.zh: 对。我没法足够强调，其实真有帮助的是也花时间和 Matilda 或谁说「那个项目落地做得好。」或「嘿，按时发布、顺利时我们有时什么都注意不到。我想让你注意，我们什么都没注意到。太棒了。你那个发布做得好。」因为那样你给了他们 positive 反馈、指出什么 work，那建关系让你有「哦对，什么 work 时他们告诉我。什么不 work 时他们也告诉我。」那也是你建信任的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They want to be criticizing them [inaudible 00:16:25]. We need to have another conversation what we're hearing about, problems [inaudible 00:16:28].
turns.zh: 他们想被批[听不清]。我们需要另一个谈话我们听到的关于问题。

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Obviously, if you say it the same way every single time, they're going to feel like this is weird. Do you recommend it's this kind of Mad Libs approach or is it make it your own as much as you can? What are kind of the key? Or is it like, here's actually how you want to say it every time?
turns.zh: 显然如果你每次同样方式说他们会觉得奇怪。你推荐这种 Mad Libs 方式还是尽量变成自己的？关键是什么？还是就这里实际是你想每次说的？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: In my book and when I work with my clients, I give specific scripts and what I will regularly say when I'm working with my clients is, "Okay, so this is how I would do it," and then I'll land it for them. But they have to make it their own. You always have to make it your own and I don't think it's a problem of doing it the same way every time. It's not like people are going to notice you because you're talking about different topics, theoretically. If you have a formula that can work for you, that's going to motivate you to do it, that is what's important. And what's important is that it's neutral, not loading on or not venting on someone and not unloading on someone.
turns.zh: 在我书里和和客户工作时我给具体话术，我经常说「好，这是我会怎么做」然后为他们 land。但他们得变成自己的。你总得变成自己的。我不觉得每次同样方式是问题。不像人会注意你因为你在谈不同话题理论上。如果你有个 formula 对你 work、激励你去做，那才重要。重要的是它是中性的，不在上面加载、不对人 vent、不对人 unload。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that we started with this one because it feels like the most common one of just your employee is underperforming and you want to make sure they understand and adjust. What if you're not hearing something from a bunch of people? What if it's just your perception of their writing? You need to work on your writing skills or you're coming in late. Is there another way you phrase it where it's not, "I'm hearing it from other people?"
turns.zh: 我喜欢我们从这个开始因为它感觉是最常见的——你员工 underperform 你想确保他们理解、调整。如果你不是从一堆人那里听到？如果只是你对他们写作的感知？你需要提升写作技能或你迟到。有没有别的方式 phrase 不是「我从别人那里听到」？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Oh, absolutely. Absolutely. So I'll talk about writing. I think it would be something like, okay, "Matilda, part of your job is to be able to create these documents and I appreciate that you do them on time. What I've observed is that they can often be not as structured as I'd like them to be and they also lack a conclusion. So what I'd love you to do is look at these three or four examples of some folks who are doing them really well and see if you can model your writing on theirs. If you need to take additional classes or if you need help in any way, let me know. But ultimately, I want to get your writing to the level where everybody is appreciating what you bring to the table because the level of your writing really reflects the level of your thinking."
turns.zh: 哦，绝对有。绝对。我说写作。我觉得会是「好，Matilda，你工作的一部分是能创建这些文档，我 appreciate 你按时做。我观察到的是它们经常没我想要的那么结构化，也缺结论。所以我想让你做的是看这三四个做得好的人的例子，看你能不能 model 你的写作于他们。如果你需要上额外课或需要任何帮助，告诉我。但最终我想让你的写作到大家 appreciate 你 bring 的水平因为你写作水平真的反映你思考水平。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Wow, I like that. I'd want to follow your advice if I got that. So the way you started that is what I've observed, which also is not like, "Here's what I think" or "Here's what you just need to do." It's more like, "Here's what I've noticed, here's what I've seen, here's what I've observed about what you're doing." And then it reminds me of, what is it, nonviolent communication, that whole framework of just focus on what you see, not what is wrong with them, not what they've done. I guess, is there anything there you want to say of just the importance of focusing on what you've heard from people or what you've observed versus maybe what people often do instead?
turns.zh: 嗯。哇，我喜欢那个。我得到那个会想 follow 你的建议。你开始的方式是我观察到的，也不像「这是我想的」或「这是你该做的」。更多是「这是我注意到的、我看到的、我观察到的关于你在做的」。然后让我想到，什么来着，非暴力沟通，那个框架就聚焦你看到的，不是他们有什么问题、不是他们做了什么。这里有什么想说的关于聚焦你从人那里听到的或你观察到的 vs 大家经常做的？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah, I mean you just really said it and I think it's such an important point, observable facts. The idea that this is not a judgment. This is not... Sort of as less judgy as possible is also very helpful. It makes it neutral. It's observable facts and it's also sort of based on expectations, right? So the writing is, we expect it to be at a certain level and it's not that way. And here are the reasons it's not, the specific reasons, it's not. (00:19:35): The way you interact with your peers, it's important to be at a certain standard, and here's why. Because when we all work together, we're going to be able to execute and when we don't, unfortunately we won't be able to. So you staying in sync with them is important and the observation is that they don't feel fully in sync with you. (00:19:52): And so every time we talk about this, it doesn't become this, "Oh, I don't know. I just feel..." By the way, some things you have to give feedback on and they are kind of a feeling and those are more difficult, but so many things if you do the work to really think about what is the observable data, I always ask my clients, what's my evidence that this is happening? And you have to spend some time thinking about it, but it's really worth it because it makes the feedback easier for you to give and easier for them to hear.
turns.zh: 对，你真的说了，我觉得是很重要的点，可观察事实。这不是判断。尽可能不 judgy 也很有帮助。让它中性。是可观察事实，也基于期望对吧？写作我们期望一定水平、它不是。这里是具体原因它不是。(00:19:35)：你和同级互动的方式，重要达到一定标准，这是为什么。因为我们一起 work 时能执行，不一起时不幸不能。所以你和他们保持同步重要，观察是他们觉得和你不完全同步。(00:19:52)：所以每次我们谈这个不变成「哦我不知道。我只是感觉……」顺便一些事你得给反馈它们确实是感觉、更难，但很多事如果你做了工作真想可观察数据是什么，我总问客户，我的证据这是在发生什么？你得花时间想，但值得因为它让反馈更容易给你给、更容易给他们听。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else along the lines of this specific type of feedback that is worth sharing before we move on to a different type of feedback?
turns.zh: 这个具体反馈类型还有什么值得分享的 before 我们转到不同类型反馈？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Well, I think just that the reason, one of the many reasons that people have gone uncomfortable giving feedback is that somebody might get defensive or they might start crying as we talked about. And so I have a script also, which is if someone gets defensive, which is it's like I'm giving you this feedback and you're getting defensive and I say, "Well, let's pause for a second. First of all, I want you to know that I'm telling you this actually, just to make you better because I know how important your career is to you. I know how important the success is to you and it's important to me too as your leader. The second thing is, my observation is that you're getting a little bit emotional. I want to know if we can continue having this conversation now or if we need to kind of pause it. At the end of the day, we really have to have this conversation and I really want to see you make changes, but I understand you might need a few moments to digest it." (00:21:18): The importance of that for you is not even what you say, but that you have prepared and you are prepared for if someone has that kind of reaction and that you don't have to, yourself, react to it. You know, "No, I'm not doing that. No, no, no, no, whatever." And you can say, "Yes, you are." Now we're in a fight and that is not cool for anybody. It's certainly not cool for you as a leader. So it gives you the opportunity to recognize that you have another tool in your toolkit rather than just react.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得大家不舒服给反馈的原因之一、很多原因之一是人可能 defensiveness 或开始哭如我们聊的。所以我也有话术，如果人 defensiveness，就是我在给你反馈、你在 defensiveness，我说「好，暂停一下。首先我想让你知道我告诉你这个其实只是让你更好因为我知道你的职业对你多重要。我知道成功对你多重要，作为你 leader 对我也重要。第二，我观察到你在变得有点情绪化。我想知道我们现在能不能继续这个对话或需要暂停一下。最终我们真得有这个对话、我真想看你做出改变，但我理解你可能需要一些时刻消化。」(00:21:18)：对你的重要性不在你说什么而是你准备了、你准备了如果人有那种反应、你不必自己 react。你知道「不我不做那个。不不不不什么的。」你说「对你。」现在我们在打架，那对谁都不好。对你作为 leader 肯定不好。所以它给你机会认识到你工具箱里还有别的工具而不只是 react。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So if you find yourself feeling defensive or they are just not hearing and just fighting back, the tool is just pause. Let's just pause for a moment and it feels like there's kind of two parts to which you just shared. One is, remind them why this is important to them and why you're talking about this. And then two is, if there's just emotions kind of taking over, give them a chance to like, "Let's just pause and maybe come back to this because maybe you're not in the right state right now to listen."
turns.zh: 所以如果你发现自己感觉 defensiveness 或他们就是不听、fight back，工具就是暂停。让我们暂停一下。感觉你刚分享的有两部分。一是提醒他们为什么这对他们重要、你为什么谈这个。二是如果情绪 takeover 了，给他们机会「让我们暂停、也许回来因为这个，也许你现在不在对的状态听。」

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，exactly。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sometimes people get upset when you mention like, "You're getting emotional," or I don't know. Is that a thing that you deal with of just like, "How dare you say I'm feeling emotional?" I'm just...
turns.zh: 有时人 upset 当你提「你在变得情绪化」或什么。那是个你处理的吗就「你怎么敢说我情绪化？」我就……

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: I'm not emotional. Why do you think [inaudible 00:22:31] emotional? Right, exactly. Yes, of course. Now, when someone's crying, they're obviously getting emotional. When they're defensive, it's possible that you might want to use a different word. I can see that this is really upsetting you or this is really triggering you, or I can see that the temperature between us has just changed. You could say something like that. I do think also it's helpful to know your people because sometimes you could realize that actually they can deal with that, but then sometimes you have to really [inaudible 00:23:00] the delicate words that you need to use to pause the conversation.
turns.zh: 我没情绪化。你为什么觉得我情绪化？对，exactly。是，当然。现在哭时显然在变得情绪化。defensiveness 时你可能想用不同词。我能看到这真的让你 upset 或这真的触发你，或我能看到我们之间温度变了。你可以那样说。我也觉得知道你的人有帮助因为有时你 realize 他们其实能 deal 那个，但有时你真得用 delicate 的词暂停对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And I find, to your point, it's helpful to you too as the person giving it. And I feel like sometimes, you may be feeling like I should just pull back and maybe I'm wrong, maybe they're right, maybe I should stop and instead this gives you a chance to know I'm actually, I can't. I need to stay strong about what I believe because I... You put so much thought and effort into this already, it's unlikely you're just like, oh, totally wrong about what you're saying.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得如你所说对你给的人也有帮助。我觉得有时你可能觉得我该 pull back 也许我错了、也许他们对、也许我该停，而这个给你机会知道我其实不能。我得对我相信的保持 strong 因为我……你已投入那么多思考和努力，不太可能你 totally 错。

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. There's something going on. There's something going on. And then also, the whole point about it being a conversation is that actually it's a conversation. Actually, Lenny, if you have a different point of view, I would like to hear it. Let's talk about it, but we can't keep going on like this, where I don't feel I can count on you for whatever it is that we're talking about. So we need to have this conversation and recreate a set of expectations between ourselves. Ultimately, that kind of conversation has the potential to really build the relationship and build trust, and that's another reason I encourage everybody to get over their discomfort and to lean into having these conversations because on the other side of that, is a much better, stronger connection.
turns.zh: 对，exactly。有什么在发生。然后也，它是对话的重点其实是它是对话。其实 Lenny，如果你有不同观点我想听。让我们谈，但我们不能这样继续，我觉得我不能指望你。所以我们需要这个对话、重建我们之间的期望。最终那种对话有潜力真建关系、建信任，那是我鼓励大家克服不舒服、leans in 这些对话的另一原因，因为另一面是更好更强的连接。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And especially if you do them well.
turns.zh: 尤其如果你做好。

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Following this advice. So okay, so again, if somebody's feeling defensive, can you again say how you start that, if you notice that? And then I'll highlight the two elements again of the...
turns.zh: follow 这个建议。好，如果人 defensiveness 你能再说怎么开始吗，如果你注意到？然后我再 highlight 两个元素……

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: So the way to pause is to actually say, "Let's just pause for a second because I'm feeling the energy has changed and I can see that you're getting a little bit heated by what I'm saying and I want you to know that I have no intention of upsetting you. I just want to be able to talk to you about the things that are going to help you in your career."
turns.zh: 暂停的方式是说「让我们暂停一下因为我觉得能量变了、我能看到你被我说的弄得有点 heated，我想让你知道我没意图 upset 你。我只是想能和你谈帮你职业的事。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And I love, again, just the reminder of here's why this is important to you, here's the benefit to you and why this will help you. And then it's like, "Okay, let's just maybe take a pause and come back to this conversation if you're feeling like this isn't the best time." Awesome. Anything else along that line before we go to another type of a hard conversation?
turns.zh: 太好了。我再次爱提醒这里为什么对你重要、对你的好处和怎么帮你。然后是「好，也许暂停一下、如果觉得不是最佳时机回来这个对话。」太好了。这条线还有什么 before 我们去另一种难对话？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: I mean, I can talk all day about this [inaudible 00:25:06], but I'm happy to move on.
turns.zh: 嗯，我能聊一天这个，但 happy move on。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let's pick another topic. I know you have kind of five buckets and types of conversation. Maybe the promotion one. That feels like I think we're in performance review season. It feels like these are happening a bunch. What do you suggest when someone's being told they're not going to get the promotion they expected or wanted?
turns.zh: 好，选另一个话题。我知道你有五桶类型对话。也许升职那个。感觉是绩效评估季。这些发生很多。你建议当有人被告知不会得到期望或想要的升职时怎么做？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Of course that's challenging. So again, getting your mindset right, recognizing they're disappointed, they're going to be disappointed, recognizing how you felt, the time that when you didn't get a promotion or whatever. And so kind of coming to it with some compassion. And also, you have to get your reasoning right. So sometimes people think they should get a promotion because they were here for a year or whatever. Sometimes people think they should get a promotion because they're the only internal candidate who's qualified for this or they might have a sense of themselves succeeding or achieving that is more inflated maybe than you see them. So trying to think about where they're coming from. (00:25:56): And then the conversation is just, "Matilda, I know this is going to be challenging for you to hear. I know you were hoping to get that promotion, but I want to let you know that we are going to actually be looking for an external candidate. I want to give you a few thoughts about why. First of all, in discussing this with my peers, I'm realizing that we need someone who has done this role multiple times in the past and has that experience. Number two, I think it's really important that they have an expertise in a specific realm that we've identified as really important. So for those reasons, we're going to bring someone in from the outside, not going to promote you, but I want you to know this. Number one, it's really important to me that you're able to succeed in your career here. And so I want to continue to help you find opportunities to build your skills and to advance. And then number two, when we bring this person in, I'm committed to finding someone who's a great people leader, who is going to help you build those skills."

turns.zh: 好了。本期节目由 Liveblocks 赞助，这个平台把你的产品变成用户想去的地方。用现成协作功能你可以用顶级公司才能完美做到的体验 supercharge 你的产品。想想 Notion 那样的 AI copilot、Figma 那样的多人、Linear 那样的评论通知甚至 Google Docs 那样的协作编辑，最小配置或维护。(00:38:31)：各行各业各阶段的公司都依赖 Liveblocks 驱动产品 engagement 和增长。今天加入他们，给用户让他们变成日活的体验。去 liveblocks.io/lenny 注册免费账号。我想稍微 tangent，触及我们聊的所有东西，就是你很强调帮 leader 理解他们的工作不是让员工开心。你工作是什么？为什么大家觉得让员工开心是他们的工作、作为 leader 该想什么？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: [inaudible 00:39:09], I work with a lot of founders and so, don't forget that the entry-level position for a founder is leader, and they have it, they often not had a lot of other experiences being a leader or a manager, and so they're just doing the best they can. It makes sense, right? And they kind of get all this information from other people and their HR leader wants to have a happy engaged workforce and they don't want to upset people for all the reasons we talked about, why you don't want to upset people. Nobody wants to upset people. (00:39:40): And so there's this idea of, they're trying to now be now be the leader who everyone loves and makes people happy. So they would often bend over backwards to make people happy, to keep people, their morale up. But what really needs to happen very often is, we need to drive towards results. And the way this system is working is not going to drive us towards results or this employee continuing to not really do a great job at their job and not really pushing themselves. And you don't want to push them because you don't want to upset them, you don't want to give them difficult feedback, so you're just going to keep hoping it works out. (00:40:23): Ultimately, that leads to the demise of your company. I mean, ultimately right, as you're a startup? If you're not in a startup and you're a large company, it still is very subpar performance, obviously. And you're dancing around hoping and praying they're going to get there and they don't really know there's a problem. And so, I think it's very misguided for leaders to have this notion that their most important role is to keep people happy, is to create this high engagement workforce. High engagement workforce is great. (00:40:56): I think what that comes from is winning culture, which means we're set up for success. We've got the structure for success, we have the culture for success, everyone understands their role, they know the impact of their role. So doing the work to figure out and help them figure out the impact of their role and that when they work together and achieve these milestones, they win and then we celebrate the wins and then we do it all over again. And when you create that kind of a workforce, I think it's much more dynamic, even though sometimes in doing that, you have to redirect people and ruffle their feathers.
turns.zh: [听不清]，我和很多创始人工作，别忘了创始人的入门职位是 leader，他们经常没很多做 leader 或 manager 的其他经验，所以他们尽力。make sense 对吧？他们从别人那里得到所有这些信息、HR leader 想要开心 engage 的员工、他们不想 upset 人因为所有我们聊的原因。没人想 upset 人。(00:39:40)：所以有这个想法，他们试图做一个人都爱、让人开心的 leader。所以他们经常 bend over backwards 让人开心、保持 morale。但很多时候真正需要的是我们朝结果推进。这个系统运作的方式不会把我们朝结果推进或这个员工继续不真正做好工作、不真正推自己。你不想推他因为不想 upset 他、不想给难反馈，所以就一直希望它好。(00:40:23)：最终那导致你公司 demise。我是说最终对吧，你是创业公司？如果你不是创业公司是大公司，仍是非常亚par的表现显然。你在周围跳、希望祈祷他们会到那、他们不知道有问题。所以我觉得 leader 有这个最重要的角色是让人开心、创造高 engagement 员工的想法很 misguided。高 engagement 员工很好。(00:40:56)：我觉得那来自赢的文化，意味着我们 set up 成功。我们有成功的结构、成功的文化、人人理解自己角色、知道角色影响。所以做工作 fi……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Essentially, the way I think about it is you think making people happy is not having hard conversations, not pushing them, when really, it's almost working backwards from, if we win and are killing it, people will be happy and what does it take to do that?
turns.zh: 本质上我想的方式是你以为让人开心是不难对话、不推他们，其实几乎从如果我们赢、killing it 人会开心 backwards work，做到那个要什么？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: A hundred percent. And then the right people are going to want to join your team, people who like to win and like to get results.
turns.zh: 一百 percent。然后对的人会想加入你团队，喜欢赢、喜欢拿结果的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story, an example of a founder you worked with or that comes to mind of this kind of where they thought this was their approach and then they shifted? Or is there kind of a pattern you see often?
turns.zh: 有没有故事、你工作的创始人的例子或这种 pattern 常见的？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: One company comes to mind. One leader I worked with. Sometimes I think to myself, if I'm writing a book, the book would start with, "It all started with the avocado toast," because he wants to do right by his workforce. And so they have avocado toast at 10 AM, like tea time kind of a thing. And it became this great ritual where people would kind of hang out together and that was great. And then that turned into other longer periods of just hanging out together. Again, these are good things. And that turned into evening socials and everybody was enjoying spending time together, but they continued to be not fully clear on what they were actually supposed to do. And there began to be kind of a cliquey, gossipy culture of who's in and who's out. And that would take up a lot of the socialization time discussions. So rather than talk about expectations about the work and about results, and again, the results were not showing. So it wasn't a lot to celebrate. (00:43:05): They started at a culture committee. So they had a culture committee to talk about how we can make people happier around here. And you can imagine there's now layers and layers of things where we're trying to focus on engagement and we're trying to focus on the employees having a great experience. And the leader I'm working with is completely sincere. It actually want to have a great workplace. But I think the misguidedness was that he hadn't done a great job setting expectations. He had not done a great job of quote unquote "codifying their culture" because culture is not just avocado toast and working together and having socials, culture is things like, we go the extra mile or culture is we make sure, or it could be, we measure twice and cut once. Those are kinds of things that are really about the way we get work done around here. And certainly, a focus on results is like, are we following the process to then get the revenue and to then build a profitable company or are we just kind of hanging out together? (00:44:07): So he had to come to terms with his own discomfort of addressing this with employees and his own discomfort in being a corporate drone of, "Oh, expectations and in the workplace and how we do things." And it turned out that's the whole thing with coaching and with working with people is that you kind of see what their underlying assumptions and beliefs are and there's a reason everyone does what they do. So there's a reason he's doing what he's doing. We had to come to terms with that and then he had to really courageously make some changes about the way he was operating. And ultimately, they had to part ways with one or two really toxic people who were creating this gossipy culture and making people feel not included and not focused on results. And then when they all got on the same page, they were able to gain a lot more traction.
turns.zh: 一个公司想到。一个 leader 我工作过。有时我想如果我写书，书会开始「一切都始于牛油果吐司」，因为他想对员工好。所以他们上午 10 点有牛油果吐司，像茶时间那种。变成很棒仪式大家聚一起，很好。然后那变成其他更长时间聚一起。这些是好东西。然后变成晚上社交，大家都享受一起待，但他们继续不完全清楚他们实际该做什么。开始有派系、八卦文化谁在谁出。那占据大量社交时间讨论。所以不是谈工作期望和结果，再说结果没显示。所以没多少可庆祝。(00:43:05)：他们开始文化委员会。所以有文化委员会讨论怎么让人更开心。你能想象现在一层一层我们试图聚焦 engagement、试图聚焦员工有很好体验。和我工作的 leader 完全真诚。真想有很好工作场所。但我觉得 misguided 是他没做好 set 期望。他没做好「codify 他们文化」因为文化不只是牛油果吐司和一起 work 和社交，文化是像我们多走一英里或我们确保、或可以是量两次切一次。那些是关于我们这里怎么完成工作的。当然聚焦结果就是，我们在 follow 流程然后拿收入、建 profitable 公司还是就在一起 hang……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like a lot of leaders and founders can relate to this, of wanting to create a great culture and keep it nice and friendly and everyone's a family and then things don't quite work out often in those cases. And there's a shift to, "Okay, we actually need to make a business that works."
turns.zh: 我觉得很多 leader 和创始人能 relate。想创造好文化、保持友好、大家是家人，然后事经常不太 work。有转变到「好我们真得做一个 work 的业务。」

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It always reminds me, Sheryl Sandberg came to talk at Airbnb once and people are asking, "What do you do with all this...? We're just constantly in chaos. Things are always reorging or changing, just never... I'm on different teams every six months. Our goals are shifting. What do you do with all this... Our culture's changing as we grow." And she's like, "That is a sign of hyper growth and success. And the opposite is even worse when you are not growing and you don't want that. And so you should be happy this is the challenge you're running into."
turns.zh: 总让我想到 Sheryl Sandberg 有次来 Airbnb 谈，大家问「你拿所有这些……我们就一直在 chaos。总 reorg 或变化，就从不……我每六个月在不同团队。目标变。你拿所有这些……我们文化随增长变。」她说「那是 hyper growth 和成功的标志。相反更糟是你不增长、你不想要那个。所以你应该 happy 这是你碰到的挑战。」

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: I love that. It's so true.
turns.zh: 我爱那个。太真。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So along these lines, you talk about how a lot of founders have to come to terms, and it's not just founders, it's just execs and leaders you work with, have to come to terms with, "Here's what I thought leadership was going to be and how to be a great leader, and here's what it really is." Is there anything more there that you find is commonly what they're wrong about or what they miss and what they have to realize?
turns.zh: 这条线你谈很多创始人得 come to terms，不只创始人是你工作的 exec 和 leader，得 come to terms「这是我以为 leadership 会是的、怎么做好 leader，这是它真是的。」有什么更多他们常错或 miss、得 realize 的吗？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah. And I think as we grow as leaders, we all have to realize our own blind spots and the difference between what we thought and what is actually going on. So I worked with a founder who she wanted to be was a visionary leader, which is fantastic. I would love that. And she was an incredibly visionary person, very inspirational. But what she didn't see is that what her company needed was somebody to structure and hold people accountable and help them create goals and achieve milestones and course correct when they got off course. And she'd be very frustrated when all those things happened. People got off course, people didn't have goals, people weren't structured to work together. But what she didn't realize was that was, in one way or the other, her job to make that happen. (00:46:49): Now, maybe she needed to have, and I would talk to her a lot about this, a partner, like a COO or somebody else who could be the person who would be sort of managing the internal while she got to be more visionary, inspirational, but ultimately, it was her job to make sure that that was in place. And she didn't sort of see that and she did not adjust her style. And so there's a lot of wheel spinning that happens from that. Even though, by the way, she was an incredibly inspirational person and incredibly inspirational leader and she meant so well. There was nothing malicious about it. It's just that she didn't see the situation for what it was and then adjust.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得我们作为 leader 成长都得 realize 自己 blind spot 和以为的 vs 实际发生的。我工作过一个创始人，她想成为 visionary leader，很棒。我会爱那个。她是非常 visionary 的人、非常 inspirational。但她没看到的是她公司需要的是有人 structure、hold 人 accountable、帮他们 create 目标、achieve 里程碑、偏了纠正。这些发生时她会很 frustrated。人偏了、人没目标、人没结构一起 work。但她没 realize 那某种程度上是她工作让那个发生。(00:46:49)：也许她需要有——我很多和她聊这个——一个 partner 如 COO 或别的可以管内部她更 visionary、inspirational，但最终她工作确保那个 in place。她没看到、没调整风格。所以很多轮子空转。即使顺便她是非常 inspirational 的人和 leader、非常真诚。没恶意。就是她没看到情况是什么然后调整。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me, we had this coach on the podcast, Joe Hudson, and he had this phrase that I think a lot of people use, but it just stuck with me. What you resist, persists. So if you hate confrontation, you're going to have much more confrontation. If you hate structure... Actually, this reminds me, Joe Gebbia at Airbnb. He was very anti-process at the beginning of Airbnb. He's like, "We're not going to have a process. I hate process. We're going to run... That's the big company stuff." And then it just chaos constantly. And then eventually it's like, "Okay, we need to have some process to how we build things."
turns.zh: 让我想到我们请过 Joe Hudson 教练上播客，他有这句话很多人用但留在我心里：你抗拒的持续。如果你恨对抗你会有更多对抗。如果你恨 structure……其实这让我想到 Airbnb 的 Joe Gebbia。他开始很反 process。就「我们不要 process。我恨 process。那是大公司的东西。」然后一直 chaos。最终「好我们得有些 process 怎么 build 东西。」

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so it's interesting. A lot of people have to realize the thing they think was bad is actually, I see why people do it this way.
turns.zh: 所以有趣。很多人得 realize 他们觉得 bad 的其实我看到为什么人那样做。

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah, totally. Actually, I'd like to say something about that because so many... Founders are kind of mavericks and they come into a situation or they start at this company and they want to do things their own way and that's fantastic. Otherwise, they wouldn't be a founder. That's actually fantastic. And so many of the founders I've worked with want to reinvent leadership. Right? They want to have it with no process, they want to have no hierarchy, they want to have autonomy, whatever it is. (00:48:37): And my feeling is like, "God bless. You should absolutely try to do that." But at the end of the day, what happens is, they kind of invent for themselves the understanding that they need to have process, hierarchy, roles and responsibilities, goals, OKRs, whatever it is. And I think it's helpful sometimes to go through that fire of thinking we can do it a different way. But ultimately, I think that the ways to structure a group of people and get them organized so that they can win, are kind of well trod. And I would say that it's helpful to get through that stage quickly so that you don't have to constantly reinvent the wheels of leadership.
turns.zh: 对，totally。其实我想说点那个因为很多……创始人是 maverick，他们进一个情况或开始这个公司想用自己的方式做，那很棒。否则他们不会是创始人。那其实很棒。我工作过很多创始人想 reinvent leadership。对吧？他们想没 process、没层级、有自主权什么的。(00:48:37)：我的感觉是「God bless。你绝对该试做那个。」但最终发生的是，他们有点为自己发明了理解他们需要 process、层级、角色责任、目标、OKR 什么的。我觉得有时经历那个火、想我们可以不同方式做是有帮助的。但最终我觉得 structure 一群人、组织他们让他们赢的方式相当 well trod。我会说快速通过那个阶段有帮助，这样你就不必不断 reinvent leadership 轮子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such an important context. Obviously, one of the... The most successful founders come up with, have first principles thinking into how to do stuff, and oftentimes they find something no one has ever thought about. So it's always this balance of try a bunch of stuff, a lot of it won't [inaudible 00:49:34]. Some of it was, what will help you win. And I think that's a really good point. I want to get into a couple more tactical things that you often work on with founders. One is, running meetings. Meetings come up a lot on this podcast. People hate them, people love them. There's some are great, some are bad, most are bad. You have some cool advice on just how to make meetings more effective and how to especially end a meeting to help you move forward. Talk about what your advice is there and just generally any advice for better meetings.
turns.zh: 那么重要的 context。显然最成功的创始人是第一性原理思考怎么做事，经常他们找到没人想过的。所以总是这个平衡试一堆、很多不[听不清]。一些是，什么帮你赢。我觉得那是个很好的点。我想进几个更战术的你常和创始人做的。一是 run 会议。会议在这播客上经常出现。人恨、人爱。有的好、有的差，大多差。你有些很酷建议怎么让会议更有效、尤其怎么结束会议帮你前进。聊你的建议和一般更好会议的建议。

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yeah. I'm one of the few people that loves meetings. Or I should say I don't love meetings. I love the potential for meetings. We have all this smart people in the room. We have the potential to talk about these great things and make decisions. And unfortunately, they don't go that way. So what happens often, I mean there's so many downfalls with meetings, but one thing that happens is, we keep meeting. Either we make decisions or we don't make decisions, but then we come back to meet again and we don't have any continuity from the last. So then we re-meet, we re-decide, and that is a big problem. So my three questions to end the meeting are, what did we decide here? Who needs to do what by when? And who else needs to know? And if you can capture those, articulate those as deliverables, I promise you, you're going to have better meetings.
turns.zh: 对。我是少数爱会议的人。或我该说我不爱会议。我爱会议的潜力。我们有所有聪明人在房间。我们有潜力谈这些 great 事、做决策。不幸的是它们不走那样。所以经常发生，会议有很多 downfall，但一件事是我们继续开。要么我们做决策要么不做，然后回来再开、上次没有连续性。所以我们重开、重决定，那是大问题。所以我结束会议的三个问题是：我们在这里决定了什么？谁需要何时做什么？还有谁需要知道？如果你能捕捉那些、articulate 那些作为 deliverable，我 promise 你会有更好会议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so it's, what did we decide here? Who's going to do what by when? So basically, action items with dates. And then, who needs to know about what we decided here? Is that how you put it?
turns.zh: 好，所以是：我们在这里决定了什么？谁要何时做什么？所以基本是带日期的 action item。然后谁需要知道我们这里决定的？是那么 phrased 吗？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Yes. Who else needs to know? There's so many executive teams that I've worked with and at first, they go into their room, they have their meeting, they make their decisions and then they leave and they don't tell anyone. "I made this promise for my team that you guys need to kind of go do." Or, "We decided on a policy of some sort and we forgot to tell everybody." And again, no, absolutely no maliciousness, just that they forget or they're too busy and there's not part of the protocol and the process inside of the company that encourages and really insists that people share important information, so cascading that down. (00:51:37): But even the first question, what did we decide here? If you really go around the room at the end of a meeting or six people in the meeting, let's say, and you say to everybody, "What did we decide here?" And they all write it down, you will get six different answers, even though we're in the same meeting. I love that it's so powerful, but also, so helpful to really raise that up, to surface that and then to figure out what to do about it.
turns.zh: 是。还有谁需要知道？我工作过很多高管团队一开始进房间、开会、做决策然后离开不告诉任何人。「我为我团队做了这个承诺你们得去做。」或「我们决定了某个政策忘了告诉大家。」再说完全没恶意、就是忘了或太忙、公司里没有鼓励和坚持大家分享重要信息的 protocol 和流程，所以 cascade 下去。(00:51:37)：但即使第一个问题我们决定了什么？如果你真在会议结束绕房间、六个人的会，你对每个人说「我们决定了什么？」他们都写下，你会得到六个不同答案即使我们在同一个会。我喜欢那个那么 powerful 但也那么有帮助真 raise 那个、surface 那个然后 figure 怎么办。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you highlighted that. I was going to say exactly the same thing, that everyone in their head has the thought of, "Here, oh yeah. Here's what we decided." And to your point, it's often not the same. So is the advice here, is this like a template or something you fill out at the end of a meeting or is it someone's job to make sure these three things happen or how do you operationalize these three questions?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你 highlight 那个。我正要说一样，每个人脑子里都有「好这是我们决定的。」如你所说经常不一样。所以这里建议是 template 还是会议结束填的或某人工作确保这三个发生或怎么 operationalize 这三个问题？

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: I like it that it's someone's job, the person that I sort of think of as the meetings are. And typically, that's somebody who enjoys follow-up, who enjoys putting lists together and putting things into boxes and whatnot, and there's usually someone like that on the team. And so then it's kind of exciting for them to be the follower upper. But one way or the other, so you could use a template. I think that actually baking it in as a ritual to the meeting, because the other thing about meetings is that we never have enough time. We go right to the end and we don't leave the five or 10 minutes at the end to make sure that we ask these three questions and make sure that we have an understanding of what the follow through is on these meetings.
turns.zh: 我喜欢是某人的工作，我想到的人是 meeting 的人。通常是享受 follow-up、享受列清单、把东西放盒子的人，团队通常有那种人。所以他们做 follower upper 挺兴奋。但不管怎样，你可以用 template。我觉得把它 bake 进会议作为仪式，因为会议另一个问题是我们从没够时间。我们到尾不留五或十分钟确保问这三个问题、确保理解 follow through。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm imagining is, say it's the product managers. Put this doc on the screen in the meeting as the meeting's ending and just have it filled out basically, and just confirm, "Does this look good to everyone?"
turns.zh: 我想象的是，比如 PM。把 doc 放屏幕上会议结束时基本填好，确认「大家觉得这个 ok 吗？」

turns.speaker: Alisa Cohn
turns.en: Love that. That's a great way to do it. By the way, with... Well, I just would say what's interesting about that is that if we ask people what did we decide here, I think there's value in just asking that question in particular because somebody might say, "We decided," I don't know, "Something." And other people would say, "No, we didn't. But that's actually a good idea. It sort of crystallizes what we did talk about in a more comprehensive way." I think there's value in raising the differences and I think there's value in stitching those together. So just putting it up on the board is good, especially if you're running short of time. turns.en: Yeah. So another one is, what kind of company culture do I think is important? "I want to have a get it done, results-focused culture where we're just executing the hell out of everything and that we're just focused on winning." (01:07:52): By the way, those two can actually exist together. But if you're pushing in one direction without the other and your co-founder is pushing the other direction without yours, it really can feel like two different companies. And that's... When I go into a situation at one of my client sites, often I will hear from the employees, "It feels like we have two different companies and two different cultures depending on whose team you're on." turns.zh: 对。另一个是我觉得什么公司文化重要？大家 definitely 创业前不谈、假设同一 page。一个创始人可能「我想有这个 great 公司人人都爱、我们都爱一起努力工作。感觉像……」用你之前的词「感觉像家人。」顺便那很好。太棒了。「我想有 get it done、结果导向文化我们就是执行一切、就聚焦赢。」(01:07:52)：顺便那两个其实可以一起。但如果你推一个方向没另一个、你联合创始人推另一方向没你的，真感觉像两个不同公司。那……我去客户现场经常听到员工说「感觉像我们有两个不同公司、两种不同文化取决于你在谁的团队。」那当然导致缺乏连贯一起 work、当然甚至就不同标准和期望。

turns.en: Absolutely. I mean, so many examples. I'm going to give two quick examples. That was my voice in my head for quite a long time, "What will become of me?" And I was living in Boston at the time.
